mainTopic: An animal in a garden: paying for benefit after a fall, how it fell, how far the exemption reaches, and רבי ירמיה's question about birth fluids
overview: The גמרא explains that רב's ruling is in a 'לא מבעיא' style. Of course the owner pays for the benefit if his animal ate the produce, and רב adds that he pays even when the produce only cushioned the animal's fall. The גמרא asks why this is not like מבריח ארי מנכסי חבירו, where no payment is owed. It answers that the garden owner did not choose to help, and he also lost his produce. Next, רב כהנא and רבא disagree about how the animal fell: slipping on its urine, or being pushed by another animal. רב כהנא limits the rule to the garden bed the animal fell into. רבי יוחנן extends it to the whole garden until the animal leaves and returns with the owner's knowledge, and רב פפא explains that leaving with knowledge is enough. Finally, the גמרא turns to an animal that went down in its normal way, and רבי ירמיה asks about damage from birth fluids. This depends on the rule of תחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס, and the question continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רב is teaching the bigger new idea: even cushioning gets paid for
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads רב's words in a 'לא מבעיא' style. Eating clearly requires payment for the benefit, and רב is adding that even when the animal was only cushioned by the produce, the owner pays for the benefit.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב is speaking in a 'no need to say' style. There is no need to say that if the animal ate, the owner pays for the benefit it got. But if it was cushioned, I might have said the garden owner is like someone who chases a lion away from his friend's property, so the animal's owner would not even pay for the benefit. רב teaches us that he does pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers an earlier question about רב's ruling by explaining that רב chose the less obvious case so he could teach something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From רב's word 'even cushioned' one might infer that if the animal ate, the owner pays full damages, which would clash with the משנה's ruling of paying only for the benefit. The גמרא says no: eating is simply the obvious case of paying for the benefit. The new point is that even plain cushioning, where the garden owner helped only by accident, still makes the animal's owner pay for the benefit.

keyTerms.meaning: 'No need to say': a style that starts with the obvious case and adds a bigger chiddush
It (the animal) was cushioned when it hit the produce
What it benefited, meaning the value of the benefit it got
One who chases a lion away from his friend's property
He teaches us (something new)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read רב as saying that eating makes the owner pay full damages. Eating pays only for the benefit, and that is the obvious case. Cushioning is the new case.

phrases.english: He is speaking in a "no need to say" style:
phrases.notes: 'He' is רב, whose ruling about the animal falling into the garden is being explained.

phrases.aramaic: לָא מִבַּעְיָא אָכְלָה – דִּמְשַׁלֶּמֶת מַה שֶּׁנֶּהֱנֵית;
phrases.english: There is no need to say that if it ate, it pays for what it benefited;
but if it was cushioned, I might say
he is like one who chases a lion away from his friend's property,
phrases.notes: This is a known rule: if you save someone's property without being asked, he owes you nothing.

phrases.english: and he does not even pay for what it benefited;
so he teaches us that he does pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers a challenge from before this section about what can be learned from רב's wording
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the statement as a 'לא מבעיא' (a smaller case leading to a bigger one)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב's words would suggest that eating pays full damages; and without his ruling one might think cushioning is exempt like מבריח ארי
steps.terutzMaskana: Eating is obviously paid for, and רב teaches that even cushioning is paid for

steps.title: Why not say cushioning really is exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: maybe the case of being cushioned really should be treated like מבריח ארי, with no payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us say that it is indeed so!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's חידוש by asking why the 'I might say' idea is not simply correct.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The comparison to מבריח ארי seemed reasonable. In both cases one person's property was saved through another person's property, and in the lion case nothing is paid. So why should cushioning be different?

keyTerms.meaning: But let us say it is indeed so

phrases.english: But let us say that it is indeed so!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rejection of the מבריח ארי comparison in step 1
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that cushioning requires payment
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The case looks like מבריח ארי, which does not require payment, so cushioning should also be exempt

steps.title: Two differences between the lion case and the garden case
steps.stepSummary: First difference: the one who chases the lion chooses to help, and the garden owner did not. Second difference: the lion-chaser loses nothing, and the garden owner loses his produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who chases a lion from his friend's property does it by choice, and this garden owner did not act by choice. Or another answer: one who chases a lion away has no loss, and this garden owner has a loss.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing that the garden case is different from the lion case in two ways.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Answer one: the lion-chaser chose to help for free, but the garden owner never agreed to anything. Answer two: the lion-chaser loses nothing of his own, but here the garden owner's produce was ruined in the process. Either difference is enough to require payment for the benefit.

keyTerms.meaning: By his own choice, knowingly
Alternatively, another answer
A loss

steps.whatToRemember: The מבריח ארי exemption applies only when the helper chose to help and lost nothing. The garden owner neither chose to help nor escaped loss, so the animal's owner pays for the benefit.

phrases.aramaic: מַבְרִיחַ אֲרִי מִנִּכְסֵי חֲבֵירוֹ – מִדַּעְתּוֹ הוּא,
phrases.english: One who chases a lion from his friend's property does it by his own choice,
but this one did not act by his own choice.
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the garden owner, who never meant to cushion anyone's animal.

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי, מַבְרִיחַ אֲרִי מִנִּכְסֵי חֲבֵירוֹ – לֵית לֵיהּ פְּסֵידָא,
phrases.english: Alternatively, one who chases a lion from his friend's property has no loss,
but this one has a loss.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַבְרִיחַ אֲרִי מִנִּכְסֵי חֲבֵירוֹ – מִדַּעְתּוֹ הוּא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Cushioning is like מבריח ארי and should be exempt
steps.terutzMaskana: The cases differ in choice and in loss, so payment for the benefit is owed
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the limits of the מבריח ארי rule. It only covers someone who helps by choice and loses nothing.

steps.title: How did the animal fall?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what exact case of falling רב's ruling is talking about.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new question asking for the exact case of the fall. It is setting up the answers that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the discussion was about what the owner pays. Now the גמרא wants the actual situation in which the animal fell into the garden.

keyTerms.meaning: How did it fall?

phrases.english: How did it fall?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new clarification about the case of רב's ruling
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact way the animal came to fall into the garden

steps.title: רב כהנא: it slipped; רבא: another animal pushed it
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא says the animal slipped on its own urine. רבא says another animal pushed it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: it slipped on its own urine. רבא said: another animal pushed it.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים each describe the case of the fall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב כהנא describes a fall that came from the animal itself, by slipping. רבא describes a fall caused by a second animal pushing it. The text here gives the two cases without explaining yet why they chose them.

keyTerms.meaning: That it slipped
Its urine
That another animal pushed it

phrases.aramaic: רַב כָּהֲנָא אָמַר: שֶׁהוּחְלְקָה בְּמֵימֵי רַגְלֶיהָ,
phrases.english: Rav Kahana said: It slipped on its own urine,
Rava said: Another animal pushed it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב כָּהֲנָא אָמַר: שֶׁהוּחְלְקָה בְּמֵימֵי רַגְלֶיהָ
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב כהנא: it slipped on its urine. רבא: another animal pushed it.

steps.title: What each view means in practice
steps.stepSummary: רבא's case (pushed) teaches the slipping case even more strongly. רב כהנא's case (slipped) means that being pushed counts as the owner's carelessness, so he pays full damages.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who says the animal was pushed by another animal holds that the rule applies all the more so when it slipped on its own urine. But the one who says it slipped on its urine holds that if another animal pushed it, the owner was careless and pays for the damage. The garden owner can tell him: you should have led them across one at a time.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the practical difference between רב כהנא and רבא from step 5.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבא, being pushed is already not the owner's fault, so slipping, which is even further from his control, is surely exempt from full damages. For רב כהנא, only slipping is truly not the owner's fault. A push means he let the animals crowd together, so he pays the full damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Another animal pushed it
It slipped on its own urine
All the more so
Was careless or negligent
To lead them across one by one

steps.whatToRemember: רבא exempts both cases from full damages. רב כהנא exempts only slipping. If another animal pushed it, the owner was careless and pays everything.

phrases.english: The one who says that another animal pushed it –
all the more so where it slipped on its urine.
And the one who says that it slipped on its urine –
but if another animal pushed it, that is negligence,
and it pays what it damaged;
phrases.notes: The words speak of the animal paying, but they mean its owner pays.

phrases.english: for he can say to him:
You should have led them across one by one.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּאָמַר שֶׁדְּחָפַתָּה חֲבֶרְתָּהּ כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the practical results of the two answers given in step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רב כהנא, an animal pushed by another shows the owner was careless, so he pays full damages. According to רבא, both pushed and slipped cases pay only for the benefit.

steps.title: רב כהנא limits the rule to the bed it fell into
steps.stepSummary: The 'pay only for benefit' rule covers only the garden bed the animal fell into. If it walked to another bed and ate, the owner pays full damages.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: The משנה taught this only for the same garden bed. But if the animal went from one bed to another bed, the owner pays for what it damaged.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא sets a limit on the משנה's rule about an animal that fell into a garden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Falling was an accident, so eating right where it landed is treated gently. Walking on to a new bed is a fresh act of eating. רב כהנא treats that as ordinary damage, so the owner pays in full.

keyTerms.meaning: They taught this only in the case of
A garden bed or row of produce
From one bed to another bed

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said: They taught this only
in that same garden bed,
phrases.notes: He means the bed the animal fell into, where the משנה says the owner pays only for the benefit.

phrases.english: but if it went from one bed to another bed –
it pays what it damaged.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בְּאוֹתָהּ עֲרוּגָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from how the animal fell to what happens after it lands.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Paying only for the benefit applies only in the bed the animal fell into. If it moves to another bed, the owner pays full damages.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן extends the exemption to the whole garden
steps.stepSummary: Even if the animal moves from bed to bed all day, the owner pays only for the benefit. This changes only once it leaves the garden and comes back with the owner's knowledge.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: Even from one bed to another, and even the whole day long, the owner pays only for the benefit, until the animal leaves and comes back with his knowledge.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן disagrees with רב כהנא and gives the exemption a much wider reach.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יוחנן, the whole stay in the garden goes back to the first accident of falling. Full liability starts only after the animal has left and returned with the owner knowing about it.

keyTerms.meaning: The entire day
Until it leaves and comes back
With the owner's knowledge or awareness

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ מֵעֲרוּגָה לַעֲרוּגָה,
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Even from one bed to another bed,
and even the entire day –
phrases.notes: The words left unsaid are 'it still pays only for the benefit.'

phrases.english: until it leaves and returns with knowledge.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר אֲפִילּוּ מֵעֲרוּגָה לַעֲרוּגָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Argues with רב כהנא's limit from step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The exemption covers the whole time in the garden. Full liability begins only when the animal leaves and returns with the owner's knowledge.

steps.title: רב פפא explains: leaving with knowledge is enough
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן's 'with knowledge' is about leaving, not returning. Once the animal leaves knowingly, it has learned where the food is, so even an unnoticed return makes the owner liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Do not say this means 'until it leaves with knowledge and returns with knowledge.' Rather, once it left with knowledge, the owner pays even if it came back without his knowledge. What is the reason? The garden owner can say: since it has learned the way, every time it slips away it will run there.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא clarifies the exact meaning of רבי יוחנן's words and gives the reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might read רבי יוחנן as requiring the owner's knowledge both when the animal leaves and when it returns. רב פפא says knowing about the leaving is enough. At that point the owner knows his animal has found this garden, so he must guard it more closely.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not say
What is the reason?
It has learned the way
It slips away or wanders off
It runs

steps.confusionAlert: 'With knowledge' is the owner's knowledge, not the animal's. And according to רב פפא, only the leaving needs his knowledge, not the return.
steps.whatToRemember: רב כהנא: full damages once the animal moves to another bed. רבי יוחנן: full damages only after it left with the owner's knowledge. רב פפא: even if it came back without his knowledge.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: Do not say
until it leaves with knowledge and returns with knowledge,
rather, once it left with knowledge –

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָזְרָה שֶׁלֹּא לְדַעַת.
phrases.english: even though it returned without knowledge.
phrases.notes: The words left unsaid are 'the owner pays full damages.'

phrases.english: What is the reason? Because he can say to him:
Since it has learned,
every time it slips away, it runs there.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא לָא תֵּימָא עַד שֶׁתֵּצֵא לְדַעַת וְתַחֲזוֹר לְדַעַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how to read רבי יוחנן's words in step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Liability begins once the animal has left the garden with the owner's knowledge, even if it returned without his knowledge, because it has learned the way there.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: an animal that went down normally
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's next case: if the animal went down into the garden in its normal way and caused damage, the owner pays full damages.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it went down in its usual way and caused damage, it pays what it damaged.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line from the משנה. This is a setup for רבי ירמיה's question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the animal did not fall. It walked in on its own, so the owner pays the full damage, not just the benefit. This plain rule is the starting point for the question that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: It went down in its usual, normal way (not by falling)

phrases.english: If it descended in its usual manner and caused damage –
it pays what it damaged.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָרְדָה כְּדַרְכָּהּ וְהִזִּיקָה מְשַׁלֶּמֶת מַה שֶּׁהִזִּיקָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the fallen-animal discussion to the משנה's next clause.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An animal that entered the garden normally and caused damage makes its owner pay full damages.

steps.title: רבי ירמיה asks about damage from birth fluids
steps.stepSummary: If the animal went down normally and gave birth there, and the birth fluids ruined produce, does the owner pay?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה asked: If it went down in its usual way and caused damage with birth fluids, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה asks a new question about the משנה's case, without an answer yet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The animal entered normally, so the owner is responsible for what it does there. But damage from giving birth is not a usual way of eating or trampling. The question is whether this damage also falls under the owner's full liability.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked (a real question of law)
Birth fluids
What is the law?

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya asked:

phrases.aramaic: יָרְדָה כְּדַרְכָּהּ וְהִזִּיקָה בְּמֵי לֵידָה, מַהוּ?
phrases.english: If it descended in its usual manner and damaged with birth fluids, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about an unusual kind of damage within the case quoted in step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the owner liable for damage caused by birth fluids when his animal entered the garden in its normal way?

steps.title: Which opinion the question depends on
steps.stepSummary: The question about the birth damage only makes sense according to the view that a case which started with negligence and ended by accident is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who says that a case which started with negligence and ended by accident is liable, don't ask this question. When should you ask it? According to the one who says such a case is exempt. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is narrowing down the question from Step 11. It explains which opinion makes the question a real question, and it is setting up the two sides that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Letting the animal into the garden was negligence (פשיעה), but giving birth there is an accident (אונס). Whoever holds that תחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס is חייב would make the owner pay, so there is no doubt for that view. The doubt only exists for the view that such a case is פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: It started with negligence and ended by accident
Negligence, carelessness
An accident, something out of a person's control
According to the one who says
Don't ask this; there is no question here

steps.confusionAlert: The 'negligence' here is letting the animal into the garden. The 'accident' is the birth itself. Don't mix up which part is which.

phrases.english: According to the one who says
that a case which started with negligence and ended by accident is liable,
phrases.notes: In our case, letting the animal into the garden was the negligence, and the birth was the accident.

phrases.english: don't ask this question;
when should you ask it?
According to the one who says
that a case which started with negligence and ended by accident is exempt;
what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא תִּיבְּעֵי לָךְ; כִּי תִּיבְּעֵי לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Refines the question from Step 11 by limiting it to one opinion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: According to the view that תחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס is פטור, is the owner exempt for the birth damage?

steps.title: The two sides of the question
steps.stepSummary: Is this an ordinary case of negligence followed by accident, so the owner is exempt? Or is the whole case negligence, because the owner should have guarded an animal about to give birth?
steps.simpleTranslation: Do we say that since it started with negligence and ended by accident, he is exempt? Or perhaps here it is all negligence: since he saw that the animal was close to giving birth, he should have guarded it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lays out the two possible ways to look at the case. The question is not answered here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one treats the birth as a true accident, which fits the 'started negligent, ended by accident' pattern, so the owner is פטור. Side two says the birth was not really an accident, because the owner could see it coming. So the whole thing counts as פשיעה, and he would be חייב even according to the view that exempts in the mixed case.

keyTerms.meaning: Do we say...? This opens the first side of a question
Or perhaps... This opens the second side
Entirely through negligence
To guard it

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that something which looks like an accident can count as negligence when the owner could have expected it.

phrases.english: Do we say:

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן דִּתְחִלָּתוֹ בִּפְשִׁיעָה וְסוֹפוֹ בְּאוֹנֶס – פָּטוּר;
phrases.english: since it started with negligence and ended by accident, he is exempt;

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא, הָכָא כּוּלַּהּ בִּפְשִׁיעָה הוּא –
phrases.english: or perhaps, here it is entirely negligence?
For since he saw
that it was close to giving birth,
he should have guarded it
phrases.notes: This is the reasoning of the second side: he could see the birth coming, so maybe it doesn't count as a surprise accident.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the two sides of the question that Step 12 narrowed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the birth count as an accident, so the owner is exempt? Or does it count as negligence, because he should have guarded an animal about to give birth?
